themes: US tax-credit eligibility and non-FEOC positioning
EV and energy storage demand growth
key_points: Battery chemicals revenue to grow from 4% (FY26) to 62% (FY30E) of total revenue
Non-FEOC structure qualifies for US tax-credit-linked demand from 2027, protecting against Chinese material restrictions
Licensed technology from MU Ionic Solutions and Morita JV provides competitive moat; qualification barriers create durable customer relationships
Dahej and Pakhajan plants are first commercial-scale battery-grade electrolyte facilities in India, addressing domestic cell manufacturing needs
Consolidated revenue/EBITDA/adjusted PAT CAGR of 45%/49%/87% over FY26-30E
Base business steady 15% compounder; leverage peaks in FY27E before gradual improvement
LiPF6 remains dominant electrolyte salt; limited near-term technology substitution risk
catalysts: Dahej and Pakhajan plant commissioning through FY27
Customer qualifications at US electrolyte makers
Domestic cell capacity ramp-up (63 GWh under development)
Balance sheet deleveraging as battery chemicals reach steady-state utilization

reports.summary: Neogen Chemicals is initiating a structural transformation from a specialty chemicals compounder into a dominant player in India's battery materials value chain. With INR 17.9 bn in capex largely committed and customer qualifications already secured, the company is positioned to capture the electrolyte opportunity as Indian cell manufacturing scales from 33 GWh today to 92+ GWh by 2027. Its non-FEOC status and licensed technology create a durable competitive moat against Chinese suppliers restricted by US tax credits from 2027 onwards.
reports.connection_narrative: India's battery manufacturing ecosystem is at an inflection point driven by three structural forces: the rapid build-out of domestic cell capacity (63 GWh under development), US tax-credit rules from 2027 that restrict cell makers from sourcing Chinese materials, and the technical impossibility of long-haul electrolyte imports due to formulation sensitivity and hazardous cargo constraints. These forces are creating an urgent need for locally qualified battery materials suppliers, a gap that has existed until now. Neogen Chemicals is uniquely positioned to capitalize on this opportunity because it combines established bromine and lithium chemistry expertise with licensed manufacturing technology from Japan's MU Ionic Solutions and a strategic salt joint venture with Morita, a non-FEOC structure that specifically qualifies it for the protected US tax-credit demand pool starting 2027. The company's Dahej and Pakhajan plants represent India's first commercial-scale battery-grade electrolyte and LiPF6 production facilities, and crucially, Neogen has already secured customer approvals by clearing final audits at three major US electrolyte makers, meaning it will capture business ahead of 2027 and retain it for years due to the high switching costs of cell-maker qualification. Within lithium-ion chemistry, LiPF6 remains the dominant salt with no material near-term alternative risk, while lithium-ion itself continues to dominate over sodium-ion and other battery chemistries for the decade-plus forecast horizon. The domestic electrolyte opportunity alone is set to expand from roughly USD 105 million today to USD 640 million by 2032, with every GWh of cell capacity requiring approximately INR 280 million in annual electrolyte demand. The most important catalyst to watch is the timing and utilization ramp of the Dahej and Pakhajan plants through FY28, as this will determine whether the company can translate its already-qualified customer base into sustained high-volume supply relationships. The key risk remains execution on the battery plant commissioning and customer ramp-up, combined with leverage peaking near 6x in FY27E, which means any delay in EBITDA generation from battery chemicals could strain the balance sheet and delay deleveraging.
